subject: ventures/open-tennis-robots
professional: a mechatronics engineer who builds two-wheel ball launchers and small field robots (BLDC wheel speed loops, MicroPython/ESP32 firmware, machine safety to ISO 13850 / ISO 13849-1), plus a tennis coach who runs ball-machine drills; first checks: do launch angle, wheel rpm and landing spot agree with independent ballistics, does the safety documentation state the real hazard envelope, does the e-stop reset need a deliberate act at the machine, will the firmware actually load on the BOM's board, and has anything been measured on hardware

evidence.correctness: Ran `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m tennisbots aim --x 9 --y -2 --speed 22 --topspin 1200`: elev 19.57, az -5.34, clearance 1.89 m, flight 1.30 s, wheels 4367/2223 rpm (same as the 2026-11-08 audit). Recomputed with my own integrator (scratchpad otr/indep.py, does not import tennisbots: semi-implicit midpoint at dt 2e-6, drag C_d 0.55 and lift C_L = 1/(2 + v/(r w)) from the sports-physics literature, contact when the centre is one radius above the court, clearance measured from the ball's underside): lands (9.000, -2.000), t 1.2993 s, clearance 1.886 m. Vacuum 20 m/s at 30 deg: 35.3119 m and 2.03874 s against v^2 sin 2a / g and 2 v sin a / g. Wheel rpm by hand: 2*22/0.85 = 51.76, 2*0.0335*125.66/0.5 = 16.84, top 4367.4, bottom 2223.4. Flat-shot wheel drop from momentum, m*eff*R^2/(2I) = 0.057*0.85*0.075^2/(2*0.00155) = 8.8% (README 8.8%). Spin-up ramp integral, 1,500 rpm/s to the 100 W corner (3,922 rpm) then constant power to 6,425 rpm: 4.82 s (README 4.8 s). README's 'lands 0.7 m off at 2.8% wheel error, 1.7 m at 6.6%' on the drill's 22 m/s 1,500 rpm shot: my integrator 0.72 m and 1.72 m. Bounce: normal COR 0.75 lies in ITF's rebound spec (135-147 cm from 254 cm gives sqrt(h2/h1) = 0.729-0.761); a sliding bounce (30, -5) m/s exits at 24.75 m/s and 284.9 rad/s, a gripping one (20, -10) at vx/(1+0.55) = 12.90 m/s rolling, both as hand-computed. Catch table cells re-run with --n 300 --seed 1: 1.5 m fixed 19%, 1.5 m at 4 m/s 91%, as published; the browser port's aim() gives the Python elevation and azimuth to every printed digit. Every recomputation passes; the 3 rather than 4 is because every efficiency, plant and return distribution under them is assumed, not measured.
evidence.completeness: 74 commits since the last audit (git log --since=2026-11-08 -- ventures/open-tennis-robots), mostly firmware estimators (wheel-drop launcher fit, ESC-lag and contact-time surveys), the drill runner, a drill builder on the page, `tennisbots serve`, the lift/agitator/trough CAD and an e-stop reset latch. Checked end to end: aim, drill (drill.example.json compiles 4 shots), catch-study, page drill builder (34 node tests), the served page (https://marisstella.app/open-tennis-robots/ returns 200 with the warranty text), `node platform/pages/served-copy.mjs open-tennis-robots` (no retired origin left), firmware handled through the simulated feeder in test_host/test_remote. Not checked here: CAD regeneration and its 'CI fails if stale' claim (build123d not installed), anything on hardware (README states openly that no robot is built). Open roadmap items 3-9 are listed as not done; netting is still not modelled.
evidence.verification: `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`: 257 tests OK in 172 s. `node --test *.test.mjs`: 34 pass in 0.7 s. Seeded 7 mutants with quality_mutate.py: Magnus constant in the inlined stepper 2.0 -> 2.6 caught; catch half-width doubled caught (both survived on 2026-11-08); launcher spin formula /(2r) -> /r caught; net-post offset from singles instead of doubles width caught; SteadyGate tolerance 3% -> 10% caught (the feed-interlock test checks release speed error 0.054 > 0.035); collector bumper rule `left > 0 or right > 0` -> `and` SURVIVED (the only bumper test drives (300, 300), so a pivot forward into the obstacle passes); controller CLEAR_ESTOP physical-button guard removed SURVIVED, but tick() re-latches from estop_pressed() on the next loop (controller.py:2407), so that mutant is close to equivalent. 5 of 7 caught, one real survivor on a safety rule. CAD's own test_cad.py (2,642 lines) not run here.
evidence.craft: Read src/tennisbots/ballistics.py, launcher.py, catcher.py, court.py, firmware/esp32/controller.py (handle, SteadyGate, SET_BASE), main.py imports, config.py constants, hardware/safety.md and electronics.md 'Reset at the machine'. Physics code is typed, unit-labelled and clear; the inlined RK4 stepper duplicates acceleration() but a test pins the two bit-identical. Defects: firmware/esp32/controller.py is 2,459 lines / 131 KB of MicroPython source in one module, cad/otr_cad/params.py 5,443 lines, firmware/esp32/README.md 3,294 lines that read as a lab notebook of simulator experiments rather than a builder's guide; tests/ holds about 60 one-off sweep scripts beside the unit tests; launcher.aim still leaves its 6-pass azimuth loop without signalling non-convergence (launcher.py:333; it reports the actual landing, so not silently wrong).
evidence.claims: Backed: catch table (two cells re-run), wheel-speed error to landing error (0.7/1.7 m recomputed), 8.8% drop, 4.8 s spin-up, 7,000 rpm = 55 m/s surface speed, ITF court and ball constants, 'no robot built', SET_BASE clamped to +/-4.0 m (controller.py:2376, test_robots:227), feed interlock at 3% (test_host gate tests; safety.md corrected from 5%), e-stop reset at the machine (electronics.md:40, test_host ResetAtTheMachineTest), pyproject Homepage and llms.txt now on marisstella.app, no-warranty text on README, safety.md and the live page. Not backed: hardware/safety.md:3 says the machine throws balls 'at up to ~30 m/s (more than 100 km/h)', but the firmware clamp MAX_RPM 7000 (controller.py:45) with 150 mm wheels and the assumed 0.85 efficiency gives 0.85*7000*2pi/60*0.075 = 46.7 m/s (168 km/h), and `tennisbots aim --x 11 --y 0 --speed 40` plans a 40 m/s shot (5,992 rpm both wheels) without complaint; feeder-catcher.md:138 sizes the netting question at '30+ m/s'. The safety document understates the hazard a builder guards against by more than half again.
evidence.fitness: A builder can plan shots, compile and check drills on a phone, size a catch net, cut and print the collector and a large part of the feeder, and run drills against a simulated board; a tennis coach gets a usable drill builder (tap balls on a court, speed/spin/pause, feed-gap estimate, shareable link) whose presets and 3 s default interval are realistic for ball-machine feeding. But nothing has been built or bench-tested: launcher efficiencies, wheel plant, ESC behaviour, ball take and the club-player return distribution are all assumed, and most of the work since the last audit refines firmware estimators against a simulated wheel that is the fitted model itself (README: 'That is the method's best case, since the simulated wheel is that model'). The firmware has never run on MicroPython or an ESP32. A tinkerer could start the build; a seller could not ship, and a coach could not yet use it on court.
evidence.domain: Flight physics follows the standard literature (constant C_d ~0.55, C_L = 1/(2 + v/(r w)), friction-limited bounce with I = 0.55 m r^2, COR within ITF's rebound range); two-wheel launcher kinematics (exit speed = efficiency x mean surface speed, topspin from the faster top wheel) and the momentum-based wheel-drop reading are sound. Departures a launcher engineer would note: no Reynolds dependence of C_d, no in-flight spin decay, no speed-dependent COR or surface variants. The new e-stop reset (latching K0 set only by a RESET button, power 0.5 s after release) follows ISO 13850's 'reset must not restart' rule; a machine-safety engineer would still ask for a risk assessment, a dual-channel or monitored K0/contactor (a welded contact goes undetected, so it is single-channel, Category B/1 thinking, against the Category 3 / PL d usual for a machine that throws objects at people), a wheel-guard interlock, and a braked stop, since the wheels coast at least 20 s. The firmware is flashed as source (firmware/esp32/README.md:20: `mpremote cp ... controller.py ...`) to an ESP32-WROOM-32 (bom-feeder-catcher.csv:5, no PSRAM); MicroPython compiles a .py on the board, and its docs advise precompiling with mpy-cross or freezing large modules for exactly this reason. mpy-cross compiles controller.py to a 28 KB .mpy here, so the fix is cheap, but as shipped it is unproven that the 131 KB module even imports on the board.

defects.what: hardware/safety.md says the feeder throws balls 'at up to ~30 m/s (more than 100 km/h)', but the firmware's MAX_RPM 7000 with 150 mm wheels and the 0.85 speed efficiency allows 46.7 m/s (168 km/h), and the planner accepts a 40 m/s shot (5,992 rpm both wheels). The safety document understates the hazard envelope a builder guards and nets against

The collector's bumper rule is untested beyond a straight drive: seeding `left > 0 or right > 0` -> `and` (a pivot forward into the obstacle allowed with the bumper pressed) leaves every test green; test_bumper_allows_only_reverse only sends (300, 300) and (-200, -200). Lead's note on spot-check: tick() (controller.py:2413) re-zeroes any forward drive while the bumper is pressed in the same loop, so the mutant issues the pivot command for microseconds, not a sustained pivot; the gap is a missing test of the handler, not an unguarded hazard

Firmware is flashed as source (`mpremote cp ... controller.py`) to an ESP32-WROOM-32 with no PSRAM; controller.py is 131 KB / 2,459 lines and MicroPython compiles a .py on the board. It has never run under MicroPython or on a board; mpy-cross compiles it to a 28 KB .mpy, which the flash steps do not use

Nothing is built or measured: launcher efficiencies, wheel plant, ESC lag, ball take and return distribution are assumed, and most of the 74 commits since the last audit tune firmware estimators against a simulated wheel that is the estimator's own model (README calls it 'the method's best case')

The e-stop reset latch is single-channel and unmonitored: a welded K0 or contactor contact goes undetected, there is no wheel-guard interlock, and the wheels coast at least 20 s after a stop; a machine-safety reviewer would expect a risk assessment and Category 3 / PL d (dual channel or a monitored safety relay) for a machine that throws balls at people
launcher.aim leaves its 6-pass azimuth-correction loop without signalling non-convergence (persists from 2026-11-08; the returned landing is the real one, so not silently wrong)

Very large modules and lab-notebook docs: controller.py 2,459 lines, cad params.py 5,443 lines, firmware README 3,294 lines of simulator experiment logs; about 60 one-off sweep scripts sit in tests/ beside the unit tests

verdict: Since 2026-11-08 every defect that audit named has been fixed or mitigated: the catch geometry and Magnus constant are now pinned (both seeded bugs that survived then are caught now), SET_BASE clamps to the rail, the feed interlock runs under test through the simulated board, the URLs moved to marisstella.app, and a latching RESET at the machine means no network command can re-power the motors after an e-stop. The physics stays right everywhere I recomputed it: an independent integrator, closed-form vacuum flight, hand wheel speeds, the wheel-drop and spin-up formulas, the landing error from wheel error, ITF's rebound range, and two re-run catch-table cells. 257 Python and 34 node tests pass, and 5 of 7 seeded bugs were caught. It still does not meet the bar, because a safety claim is wrong: safety.md gives the top ball speed as about 30 m/s, while the firmware allows 46.7 m/s and the planner will plan 40 m/s. Fitness also stays at 2. Nothing has been built, the firmware has never run on MicroPython (a 131 KB source copied to a board without PSRAM), the bumper rule is tested only for a straight drive, and most of the recent work tunes estimators against their own simulated model. The design is deep and honest about its limits, but it is not yet something a launcher builder or a machine-safety engineer would sign off for use near people.
